title: Workflows, agents and who owns the control flow

items.stem: Which statement correctly tells a workflow apart from an agent?

options.text: A workflow calls tools from code, while an agent only writes text
In a workflow the code sets the steps; in an agent the model does
A workflow has no model in it, while an agent has one model
In a workflow the model sets the steps; in an agent the code does

items.stem: A makerspace booking feature runs the same code every time: (1) look up the student's training record, (2) if untrained, stop and send the sign-up link, (3) otherwise check the calendar, (4) make one model call to write a friendly confirmation. Which description fits it best?

options.text: An agent, because it contains a call to a language model
An agent, because it uses tools such as the calendar lookup
A workflow, because the code fixes the path and the model only writes step 4
A workflow, because it has fewer than ten steps in total

items.stem: Your team has a small model budget. Which part of the makerspace assistant is the best candidate for a fixed workflow rather than an agent?

options.text: Diagnosing a machine fault that the manuals do not list, from a student's description
Answering open questions that may need any manual, the calendar, or both
Planning a project that needs several machines in an order no one knows yet
Turning a request with machine, date and time into a booking, with the same checks each time

items.stem: A fixed workflow handles a booking request with exactly 3 model calls. An agent handling the same kind of request averages 5 model calls. Assume every model call costs $0.01. How much more, in dollars, does the agent cost than the workflow over 200 requests?
In one or two sentences: for a task whose steps are known in advance, why is a fixed workflow usually cheaper and more predictable per request than an agent?
In one sentence: what is one sign that a task needs an agent instead of a fixed workflow?
